comparison: Both support claims about iridescence properties (C2-C4, C30). OpenEval provides detailed statistical validation (PERMANOVA analyses), while peer reviewers accept these as foundational data within a 'state-of-the-art approach.' Peer review also includes C85 (iridescence comparison to other species) which OpenEval addresses separately in R12.

Both support visual convergence in sympatry and divergence in allopatry (C5-C6, C34-C35). OpenEval provides specific statistical evidence (PCA, PERMANOVA p<0.01 allopatry, p=0.084 sympatry) and notes the predation inference is reasonable but speculative. Peer reviewers provide 'solid evidence' for visual similarity and note predation hints 'but alternative explanations are possible.' Peer review also includes chromatic distance claims (C7-C8) which OpenEval addresses in R3.

OpenEval R3 addresses chromatic distance calculations (C7-C8, C98) showing allopatric contrasts >1 JND and sympatric <1 JND, finding this supported by receptor-noise modeling. Peer R2 includes these claims within broader visual convergence evidence, accepting them as part of 'solid evidence' for similarity in sympatry.

Both address intraspecific mate discrimination (C9-C11). OpenEval provides detailed statistical support (Fisher's exact test p=0.04, binomial GLMMs) showing asymmetric preferences between subspecies. Peer reviewers describe behavioral experiments as 'well-designed' and 'integrative' without specific concerns. Peer R3 also includes artificial modification experiments (C12-C16) which OpenEval addresses separately in R5.

OpenEval R5 addresses artificial modification experiments (C12-C16) with UNCERTAIN evaluation, noting statistical support (p<0.01) but acknowledging potential artifacts from black marker modifications. Peer R3 groups these with other behavioral experiments as part of well-designed approach without raising artifact concerns, suggesting stronger confidence than OpenEval.

Perfect agreement on interspecific discrimination in sympatry (C17-C20, C37). Both support that males fail to discriminate heterospecific females in sympatry. OpenEval provides detailed statistics (M. helenor p=0.416, M. achilles p=0.032 with weak effect). Peer reviewers explicitly affirm this 'reinforces the idea that visual signal convergence is primarily driven by predation pressure.'

Both support chemical divergence between species (C21-C24). OpenEval provides detailed evidence (nMDS, PERMANOVA p<0.001, stronger in males). Peer reviewers affirm 'increased chemical differences' and 'potential role in facilitating species recognition.' Peer R5 also includes beta-ocimene identification (C25-C26) which OpenEval addresses in R8.

OpenEval R8 addresses beta-ocimene identification (C25-C27) as supported by GC-ToF-MS analysis. Peer R5 includes these claims within broader chemical divergence findings, accepting the chemical analysis as part of the 'inclusion of both visual and chemical signals.'

Both address the escape mimicry/predation mechanism (C28-C29, C35, C93). OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN, noting the pattern is well-supported but mechanism remains speculative requiring direct predation experiments. Peer reviewers are more accepting, stating similarity 'hints to an evolutionary response to shared predators (but alternative explanations are possible)' and findings 'reinforce the idea' of predation-driven convergence.

Perfect agreement on chemical compensation hypothesis (C36, C38, C100, C106). Both support that chemical divergence compensates for visual convergence to maintain species recognition. OpenEval notes the inference is logical but direct olfactory discrimination experiments would strengthen it. Peer reviewers explicitly endorse that 'difference in chemical signaling likely helps to avoid between-species mating in sympatry.'

OpenEval R11 addresses behavioral differences between species in the field (C31-C33) as supported by citations, with speculation about differential predation pressures. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific claims.

Both address iridescence properties and selective pressures (C85, C89, C94). OpenEval supports claims about non-directional iridescence and limited sexual selection based on reflectance measurements. Peer reviewers accept the 'careful consideration of multiple selective pressures' without questioning this interpretation. Peer R9 also includes C95 which OpenEval doesn't explicitly address.

Perfect agreement on population-level courtship differences (C96-C97). OpenEval supports these claims based on behavioral observations, though notes sample sizes and statistical tests not explicitly provided. Peer reviewers describe behavioral data as 'well-designed and thorough' without concerns about these findings.
OpenEval R14 addresses measurement repeatability validation (C78-C79) as supported by rptR analysis. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these methodological validation claims.

OpenEval R15 addresses courtship motivation controls (C80, C83) as supported by statistical tests showing similar motivation across groups. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these control experiment claims.
OpenEval R16 addresses phylogenetic context (C1) as supported by citation to Chazot et al., 2021. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for this background claim.
OpenEval R17 addresses thermoregulation hypothesis (C90-C92) as supported by citations ruling out thermoregulation as primary driver. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these claims.

Perfect agreement on main conceptual conclusions (C109-C110). Both support the synthesis about multimodal communication and signal evolution. OpenEval notes this is well-supported but remains a hypothesis requiring further testing. Peer reviewers affirm the study 'broadens our understanding of multimodal communication' and 'interactions between ecological pressures and signal evolution may shape species coexistence.'

OpenEval R19 addresses methodological controls and observations (C82, C84) about experimental protocols and male approach behavior. No corresponding peer review evaluation found for these specific methodological details.

Peer R9 addresses C95 (claims about selective pressures) as part of accepting the study's consideration of multiple selective pressures. OpenEval includes C95 context within R12 discussion of C94 but doesn't explicitly evaluate C95 as a separate claim.
